statement: One bus leaves every 12 minutes and another every 18 minutes. They leave together at 9:00. When do they next leave together?

choices.misconception: I found the greatest common divisor of 12 and 18 instead of the least common multiple.
I added the two intervals together rather than looking for a time that is a multiple of both.
I found a common multiple but not the least one, landing on a later coincidence.
I multiplied the two intervals together instead of finding their least common multiple.

hints: List the departure times for each bus.
You want the first time that is a multiple of both intervals. Listing the multiples of each and finding the first one they share is quicker than any formula at these sizes.
Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36. Multiples of 18: 18, 36. The first shared one is 36 minutes, so 9:36.

solutions.reliable: List the minutes after 9:00 at which each bus leaves. The first bus goes at 12, 24, 36, 48; the second at 18, 36, 54. The first time both appear is 36 minutes, so they next leave together at 9:36. The transferable idea: two repeating cycles coincide at their least common multiple.
solutions.elegant: 12 = 2 x 2 x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3 x 3, so the least common multiple is 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 = 36.

whyOnTest: Coinciding cycles is the standard dressing for least common multiple, and reaching for the greatest common divisor instead is the reliable error.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
